title: The pigeons and the hunter
hookLine: a hunter caught in a storm shelters under the tree where he just trapped a pigeon, and her mate decides he is a guest
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is as God
tomorrow: a snake, Death and Time: who is really to blame?

cards: A storm breaks over the forest. A hunter, a hard man who lives by trapping birds, is caught out in it, soaked and shaking with cold. In his cage is a female pigeon he caught that day.
He crouches under a big tree for shelter, not knowing the tree is her home. Up in its branches her mate is grieving, wondering where she's gone. And from inside the cage, she can hear him.
Yudhishthira had asked about a person who gives shelter to someone who asks for it. This is the story Bhishma tells.

teach.b: The female pigeon calls up to her mate, and what she says is startling. Don't grieve for me. This man has come to our home, cold and hungry.
He's our guest. Treat him as one. And the male pigeon does.

He brings an ember and dry leaves and makes a fire so the hunter can warm himself. Then he realizes he has nothing to feed his guest. So he offers himself, and drops into the fire, so the hunter will have food.
The hunter is undone. The man who caught birds for a living has just watched a bird give its life to feed him. He opens the cage and lets the female go.
But she, grieving her mate, follows him into the fire, and the story says the two rise to heaven together, shining.

teach.h: THE HUNTER LAYS DOWN HIS NETS
teach.b: The hunter throws away his nets and his cage and goes into the forest to live in austerity. The word underneath all this is atithi, the guest.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS AS GOD
teach.b: An old Hindu teaching, from the Taittiriya Upanishad, says atithi devo bhava: let the guest be to you as a god. In Bhishma's telling, that reaches even the one who hurt you.

It's why, in so many Hindu homes, a visitor is handed water before much else is said, and nobody leaves without being offered food. The story is extreme on purpose; Bhishma isn't asking anyone to leap into fires.
He's showing how far the welcome reaches: all the way to the person who did you harm.

how: Hindu teaching treats the guest, atithi, as someone to be honored, and a line from the Taittiriya Upanishad, 'atithi devo bhava', let the guest be as a god, names the same ideal; Bhishma's story of the pigeons is retold as an illustration.

o: a fire lit to warm a traveler in a storm
a hunter who lives by trapping forest birds
a guest, honored whoever comes to the door

games.q: the pigeons and the hunter — tap the pairs.
p: makes a fire, then gives himself

s: the hunter sheltered under the pigeons' own tree
he didn't know the tree was the home of the bird he'd caught.
the female pigeon begged her mate to attack the hunter
she told him the hunter was their guest and must be honored.
atithi devo bhava means honor only the guests who are kind to you
it means let the guest be as a god; the pigeons honored even the hunter who trapped them.

games.q: you're the male pigeon. the man who trapped your mate is shivering under your tree, and she says he's your guest. what do you do?
o: fly away and leave him to the storm.
make him a fire, and give him what food you have.
wait for him to sleep and free your mate.
games.why: he makes a fire, and having no food, gives himself; the hunter, undone, frees the female and gives up hunting.

practice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind someone who will come through your door, or into your day, who isn't easy to welcome.

Picture doing what so many Hindu homes do first: handing them a glass of water, offering a seat, giving them your full attention. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with goodwill.

wordCard.voice: atithi. Guest: the one who comes to your door, to be honored as a god, whoever they are, even the person who hurt you.
